newsitem.title: BELGIUM: MEPs want EU-wide response to epidemics.
newsitem.headline: MEPs want EU-wide response to epidemics.

text.p: The European Parliament is expected to push on November 13 for a central agency to control the spread of diseases like tuberculosis and Creutzfeldt Jakob Disease.

According to a report by French Union for Europe MEP Christian Cabrol, which is due to be adopted by the parliament next week, the member states' reaction to mad cow disease and its human equivalent Creutzfeldt Jakob Disease (CJD) illustrates the need for an EU-wide early warning system and coordinated action to prevent epidemics.
"The general public can only view with alarm the disorderly and incoherent reactions which the (mad cow-CJD) crisis has produced," the report says.
"We want a central monitoring agency, like the one in the United States," an official with the parliament's committee on public health told Reuters.
A European Commission proposal to create a network of national monitoring agencies would not be enough to prevent the spread of contagious diseases and illnesses, the official said.

A network might be cheaper and would respect the member states' reluctance to hand over power to the EU in health matters but the system could not work effectively when only some of them actually had a national agency, she said.

As Cabrol's report makes clear, it is futile for one member state conscientiously to check the health of travellers from non-EU countries where there are outbreak of serious diseases like ebola (Zaire), legionnaires' disease (the U.S.) or bubonic plague (India) if there are no checks in neighbouring EU states.
"Since there are no longer any frontiers between the EU member states, a contagious person may infect the people of the very country which has conscientiously checked passengers," the report says.

Even in those member states which do possess a national surveillance agency, the monitoring and disease control methods vary, so it is impossible to compare the data and combat the spread of epidemics effectively. Some diseases are not monitored at all, Cabrol's report says.

Cabrol, a doctor, argues that if the member states can see the logic of having a European centre for monitoring the spread of AIDS (set up in 1987), then they should adopt a similar approach to other communicable diseases.
The Commission had not suggested such an approach for fear EU health ministers would reject it, the committee official said.
While Cabrol welcomes the Commission's proposal for a network -- COM(96)78 -- as a first step, he is doubtful whether it will achieve its aim and is proposing amendments to strengthen it.
One of the draft decision's major weaknesses is the absence of provisions for an early warning system for passing on to member state authorities details of emerging or recurring diseases.
Cabrol also doubts whether, in the absence of a central monitoring system, the draft decision will succeed in getting the member states to react quickly to health risks.

"The member states, which in the case of BSE have demonstrated their inability to react in a coherent fashion in order to protect human health, still retain their full powers so to speak in the case of the (surveillance) network," the report points out.

EU health ministers have already said they will reject a provision in the proposal which would enable the Commission to decide what protective measures to adopt in emergency situations, particularly at the EU's external borders.

"Certain member states which object to the role of the Commission should be reminded that they themselves accused the latter of not having taken the necessary action to ban imports of contaminated (cattle) feed in good time when the Commission did not actually have the power to do so," the report says.
Finally, Cabrol wants the Commission to state more clearly how it expects the surveillance network to be financed.
"If certain member states are unable to meet this financial obligation, the entire system will collapse," he warns.
